claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Doeven et al., 2004.

claims.claim: SBD1 and SBD2 bind amino acids.
claims.source: Second, the selected SBPs belong to Type I and Type II ABC importers with extensively characterized substrate (cognate and non-cognate) interactions, such as metal ions (PsaA) (McDevitt et al., 2011), sugars (MalE) (Ferenci et al., 1986), peptides (OppA) (Doeven et al., 2004), amino acids (SBD1 and SBD2) (Fulyani et al., 2016), and compatible solutes (OpuAC) (Wolters et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Fulyani et al., 2016.

claims.claim: OpuAC binds compatible solutes.
claims.source: Second, the selected SBPs belong to Type I and Type II ABC importers with extensively characterized substrate (cognate and non-cognate) interactions, such as metal ions (PsaA) (McDevitt et al., 2011), sugars (MalE) (Ferenci et al., 1986), peptides (OppA) (Doeven et al., 2004), amino acids (SBD1 and SBD2) (Fulyani et al., 2016), and compatible solutes (OpuAC) (Wolters et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Wolters et al., 2010.

claims.claim: Labeling and surface-immobilization of the protein molecules did not alter the ligand dissociation constant KD.
claims.source: Labeling and surface-immobilization of the protein molecules did not alter the ligand dissociation constant KD (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the KD values in Table 1 comparing labeled and unlabeled proteins.

claims.claim: Steady-state anisotropy measurements indicate that the dyes retain sufficient rotational freedom.
claims.source: Steady-state anisotropy measurements indicate that the dyes retain sufficient rotational freedom (Table 2) so that relative inter-dye distance can be assessed via the apparent FRET efficiency of freely diffusing or surface-immobilized protein molecules.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the anisotropy data in Table 2.

claims.claim: Saturating concentrations of cognate substrate shift the FRET efficiency histograms to higher values compared to the ligand-free SBPs.
claims.source: Saturating concentrations of cognate substrate, above the KD (Table 1), shift the FRET efficiency histograms and the fitted Gaussian distributions to higher values compared to the ligand-free SBPs (Figure 2B–G; Supplementary file 3), indicating a reduced distance between the SBP lobes and inferred to be closure of the proteins.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B-G and Supplementary file 3.

claims.claim: Higher FRET efficiency indicates a reduced distance between the SBP lobes and closure of the proteins.
claims.source: Saturating concentrations of cognate substrate, above the KD (Table 1), shift the FRET efficiency histograms and the fitted Gaussian distributions to higher values compared to the ligand-free SBPs (Figure 2B–G; Supplementary file 3), indicating a reduced distance between the SBP lobes and inferred to be closure of the proteins.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the FRET principle and the data in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Ligand-induced opening and closing transitions were observed in individual surface-immobilized SBPs in the presence of ligand concentrations at the respective KD value.
claims.source: For individual surface-immobilized SBPs, we observed ligand-induced opening and closing transitions in the presence of ligand concentrations at the respective KD value (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The solution-based FRET distributions of ligand-bound and ligand-free SBPs are unimodal and do not reveal substantial conformational heterogeneity.
claims.source: The solution-based FRET distributions of ligand-bound and ligand-free SBPs are unimodal and thus do not reveal any substantial conformational heterogeneity, such as a pronounced closing in the absence of substrate or a substantial population of an open-liganded state (vide infra).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the FRET histograms in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Ligands are bound via an induced-fit mechanism.
claims.source: This strongly suggests that ligands are bound via an induced-fit mechanism, unless dynamics occur on timescales faster than milliseconds.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the unimodal FRET distributions and the absence of substantial open-liganded states.

claims.claim: Substrate-induced SBP closing follows first-order kinetics for OppA.
claims.source: This inference was confirmed for OppA by examining individual surface-immobilized proteins and demonstrating that substrate-induced SBP closing follows first-order kinetics while the opening obeys zeroth-order kinetics (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) (Kim et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and supported by citation to Kim et al., 2013.

claims.claim: The opening of OppA obeys zeroth-order kinetics.
claims.source: This inference was confirmed for OppA by examining individual surface-immobilized proteins and demonstrating that substrate-induced SBP closing follows first-order kinetics while the opening obeys zeroth-order kinetics (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) (Kim et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and supported by citation to Kim et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Multiple substrate-bound SBP conformations exist for SBD1, SBD2 and MalE.
claims.source: Further examination of the FRET distributions shows that multiple substrate-bound SBP conformations exist for SBD1, SBD2 and MalE (Figure 2D–F).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D-F.

claims.claim: Asparagine and glutamine stabilize distinct conformations in SBD1.
claims.source: For the amino acid binding-proteins SBD1 and SBD2, the cognate substrates (Fulyani et al., 2016) asparagine and glutamine for SBD1, and glutamine and glutamate for SBD2 all stabilize a distinct protein conformation, as shown by the FRET efficiency histograms and fitted Gaussian distributions (Figure 2E–F; Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E and Supplementary file 3.

claims.claim: Glutamine and glutamate stabilize distinct conformations in SBD2.
claims.source: For the amino acid binding-proteins SBD1 and SBD2, the cognate substrates (Fulyani et al., 2016) asparagine and glutamine for SBD1, and glutamine and glutamate for SBD2 all stabilize a distinct protein conformation, as shown by the FRET efficiency histograms and fitted Gaussian distributions (Figure 2E–F; Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2F and Supplementary file 3.

claims.claim: Asparagine binding reduces the inter-dye distance in SBD1 by ~9 Å.
claims.source: Notably, closure of SBD1 by asparagine reduces the inter-dye distance compared to the ligand-free protein by ~9 Å (Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Supplementary file 3.

claims.claim: Glutamine binding reduces the inter-dye distance in SBD1 by ~5 Å, suggesting only partial closing.
claims.source: In contrast, glutamine binding reduces the distance by ~5 Å, suggesting that only a partial closing of SBD1 occurs.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Supplementary file 3.

claims.claim: Glutamine binding reduces the inter-dye distance in SBD2 by ~9 Å.
claims.source: In SBD2, glutamine and glutamate reduce the distance ~9 and ~7 Å, respectively (Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Supplementary file 3.

claims.claim: Glutamate binding reduces the inter-dye distance in SBD2 by ~7 Å.
claims.source: In SBD2, glutamine and glutamate reduce the distance ~9 and ~7 Å, respectively (Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Supplementary file 3.

claims.claim: At least three distinct ligand-bound MalE conformations exist.
claims.source: Comparison of the FRET efficiency histograms of the different MalE-ligand complexes shows that at least three distinct ligand-bound MalE conformations exist (Figure 2D; Figure 2—figure supplement 3A; Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A, and Supplementary file 3.

claims.claim: Some cognate substrates did not induce a unique MalE conformation.
claims.source: In contrast to SBD1 and SBD2, some cognate substrates did not induce a unique MalE conformation (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claims.claim: Maltopentaose and maltohexaose elicit the same FRET change in MalE.
claims.source: For example, maltopentaose and maltohexaose elicited the same FRET change, and triggered the formation of a partially closed MalE conformation with a ~7 Å reduction in the inter-dye distance.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2D and Supplementary file 3.

claims.claim: Maltopentaose and maltohexaose trigger formation of a partially closed MalE conformation with a ~7 Å reduction in the inter-dye distance.
claims.source: For example, maltopentaose and maltohexaose elicited the same FRET change, and triggered the formation of a partially closed MalE conformation with a ~7 Å reduction in the inter-dye distance.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Supplementary file 3.

claims.claim: Maltose, maltotriose and maltotetraose induce a fully closed form of MalE with a ~10 Å reduction in the inter-dye distance.
claims.source: This conformational state is different from the fully closed form of MalE, induced by maltose, maltotriose and maltotetraose, wherein the inter-dye distance is reduced by ~10 Å.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Supplementary file 3.

claims.claim: Maltoheptaose induces a partially closed MalE conformation with a ~5 Å reduction in the inter-dye distance.
claims.source: Further, it is also distinct from the other partially closed conformation induced by maltoheptaose where the inter-dye distance is reduced by ~5 Å.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Supplementary file 3.

claims.claim: The four examined cognate substrates of OppA elicit the same FRET change.
claims.source: However, whether this conformational plasticity is a universal feature among SBPs needs to be investigated further, because in OppA the four examined cognate substrates (Doeven et al., 2004) elicited the same FRET change (Figure 2G; Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claims.claim: The findings on conformational changes for each SBP were shown to be statistically robust by the non-parametric two-way Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) test.
claims.source: The findings on the conformational changes (and differences) for each SBP were shown to be statistically robust by the non-parametric two-way Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) test (p-values in Supplementary file 1), which indicates the absence of any fitting bias.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text with p-values provided in Supplementary file 1.

claims.claim: Although the examined SBPs have a single open conformation, a productive interaction between the SBP and the translocator does not require a single, unique closed SBP conformation.
claims.source: Taken together, these data indicate that although the examined SBPs have a single open conformation, a productive interaction between the SBP and the translocator does not require a single, unique closed SBP conformation.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the FRET data showing multiple conformations that support transport.

claims.claim: The structural flexibility of the SBP permits the formation of one or more ligand-bound conformations, all of which are able to interact with the translocator and initiate transport.
claims.source: The structural flexibility of the SBP permits the formation of one or more ligand-bound conformations, all of which are able to interact with the translocator and initiate transport (Fulyani et al., 2016; Wolters et al., 2010; Ferenci, 1980; McDevitt et al., 2011; Doeven et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion supported by the FRET data and citations to transport studies.

claims.claim: In ligand-free MalE, PsaA and OpuAC, no transitions to higher FRET states were observed within a total observation time of >8 min for each SBP.
claims.source: For ligand-free MalE, PsaA and OpuAC, no transitions to higher FRET states were observed within a total observation time of >8 min for each SBP (Figure 3B–D; Supplementary file 4).

results.result: Single-molecule FRET reveals that SBPs exhibit conformational plasticity, with multiple distinct ligand-bound conformations that can all activate transport. MalE shows at least six different ligand-bound conformations, SBD1 at least four, and SBD2 and OpuAC at least three. Different cognate substrates stabilize distinct conformations in SBD1 and SBD2, while some cognate substrates induce the same conformation in MalE. OppA shows a single conformation for all cognate substrates tested. These findings challenge the traditional binary open/closed model and demonstrate that multiple conformations are translocation competent.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C72 and C151-C157 are strongly supported by extensive smFRET data presented in Figures 2, 2-supplements, and Supplementary file 3. The FRET efficiency histograms clearly show multiple distinct peaks for different ligands with the same SBP, and statistical robustness is demonstrated by Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests (C70). The conclusion that multiple conformations activate transport (C71, C72, C157) is supported by the fact that all tested cognate substrates are known to be transported despite inducing different conformations. The data are internally consistent across multiple labeling positions (C47, Figure 2H, Figure 2-supplement 4).

results.result: The smFRET methodology is validated and demonstrates that cognate substrate binding induces closure of SBPs via an induced-fit mechanism. Labeling and surface immobilization do not alter ligand binding affinity (KD values in Table 1), dyes retain sufficient rotational freedom (Table 2), and saturating substrate concentrations shift FRET efficiency to higher values indicating closure. Solution-based FRET distributions are unimodal, suggesting induced-fit binding rather than conformational selection. For OppA, closing follows first-order kinetics while opening follows zeroth-order kinetics.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C55 are well-supported by the methodological validation data in Tables 1-2 and Figure 2-supplement 1-2. The comparison of KD values between labeled and unlabeled proteins (C47) provides direct evidence that the labeling strategy does not perturb function. The anisotropy measurements (C48) validate the FRET approach. The unimodal distributions (C52) and kinetic analysis for OppA (C54-C55) provide strong evidence for the induced-fit mechanism (C53). The methodology is rigorous and appropriately controlled.

results.result: Intrinsic conformational dynamics vary among SBPs. MalE, PsaA, and OpuAC show no transitions to higher FRET states in the absence of ligand over >8 minutes of observation. In contrast, SBD1, SBD2, and OppA exhibit rare transitions to high FRET states (2-8 times per minute) with average lifetimes of 205±36 ms, 90±11 ms, and 211±42 ms, respectively. Control experiments with varying concentrations of unlabeled protein confirm these represent intrinsic closing rather than contamination artifacts. This demonstrates diversity in the conformational dynamics of ligand-free SBPs.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C82 and C184 are supported by the surface-tethered smFRET data in Figure 3 and Supplementary file 4. The control experiments with unlabeled protein (Figure 3-supplement 2) effectively rule out ligand contamination as an explanation for the observed transitions (C79). The long observation times (>8 min) and large number of molecules analyzed provide statistical power. The conclusion of diversity in intrinsic dynamics (C82) is well-justified by the clear differences between proteins. However, the caveat about temporal resolution (C81) is appropriately noted.

results.result: Non-cognate ligands induce diverse conformational changes in SBPs, ranging from no change (arginine/lysine binding to SBD1, arginine to SBD2) to minor opening (carnitine-OpuAC), partial closing (histidine-SBD1, various maltodextrins-MalE, proline-OpuAC), or full closing (Zn²⁺-PsaA). Some non-cognate ligands induce conformations similar to cognate substrates (e.g., maltooctaose and maltodecaose induce similar MalE conformations as maltoheptaose; Zn²⁺ and Mn²⁺ induce similar PsaA conformations). Transport assays confirm that histidine, lysine, and arginine are not transported by GlnPQ but can inhibit uptake of cognate substrates. The degree of SBP closing alone cannot discriminate cognate from non-cognate substrates.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C110 are strongly supported by the comprehensive FRET data in Figure 4 and transport assays in Figure 4A-C. The ensemble FRET measurements (Figure 4-supplement 1) and competitive inhibition experiments (Figure 4-supplement 2) provide additional validation. The conclusion that SBP closing alone cannot discriminate cognate from non-cognate substrates (C109) is well-justified by the observation that similar conformations can be induced by both types of ligands. The data are internally consistent and statistically robust (Supplementary file 1).

results.result: The opening kinetics of PsaA dictate transport specificity for PsaBCA. Mn²⁺-bound PsaA opens rapidly (<few seconds) upon EDTA addition, while Zn²⁺-bound PsaA remains closed for >15 minutes. The D280N mutation in PsaA accelerates opening of the Zn²⁺-bound complex without altering the closed conformation. Cellular Zn²⁺ accumulation increases in S. pneumoniae expressing PsaA(D280N) but not wild-type PsaA, demonstrating that altered conformational dynamics render ligand release permissive for transport of non-cognate Zn²⁺. This shows that transport specificity is dictated by SBP opening kinetics rather than the translocator directly sensing the metal ion.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C125 are strongly supported by the FRET data in Figure 5A-C and the cellular accumulation data in Figure 5D. The experimental design elegantly tests the hypothesis by using a mutation that alters opening kinetics without changing the closed conformation (C120-C121). The ICP-MS measurements of cellular Zn²⁺ (C122) provide direct functional evidence. The conclusion that opening kinetics dictate specificity (C125) is well-justified, though the alternative hypothesis about translocator control (C118) is appropriately acknowledged. Statistical significance is demonstrated (p<0.005 and p<0.0001 in Figure 5D).

results.result: For MalE, maltoheptaose (cognate), maltooctaose, and maltodecaose (both non-cognate) induce similar conformations and have similar opening kinetics (mean lifetimes 328±8 ms, 319±12 ms, and 341±8 ms, respectively; p=0.68 by ANOVA). Since only maltoheptaose is transported, the failure to transport maltooctaose and maltodecaose cannot be explained by slow SBP opening or inefficient ligand release. Instead, this most likely originates from size limitations of the MalFGK2 translocator, as supported by analysis of binding cavities in the crystal structure showing the transporter could only accommodate maltodextrins as large as maltoheptaose.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C134, C179-C181 are well-supported by the surface-tethered smFRET data in Figure 6A-D and Figure 6-supplements 1-2. The statistical analysis (ANOVA, p=0.68) appropriately demonstrates no significant difference in opening kinetics (C133). The conclusion about translocator size limitations (C134, C179) is supported by citation to structural data (Oldham et al., 2013) and is a reasonable inference from the functional data. However, this remains somewhat speculative as direct structural evidence for the size exclusion mechanism is not provided in this study. The alternative explanations are appropriately ruled out by the data.

results.result: Altering SBP conformational dynamics by mutation affects transport activity. The MalE(A96W/I329W) mutant opens almost three orders of magnitude slower than wild-type (28±5 s vs 63±6 ms), and this correlates with reduced maltose-stimulated cellular growth and ATPase activity. A negative correlation exists between SBP lifetime and transport activity when conformational dynamics are altered by mutation (as also observed for GlnPQ and PsaA(D280N)). This demonstrates that for ligands inducing highly stabilized SBP-substrate conformations requiring more energy to open, transport becomes slower or is abrogated.
results.evaluation: Claims C135-C139, C169-C170, C177 are supported by the smFRET data in Figure 6A and Figure 6-supplement 3, combined with published functional data (citations to Gould et al., 2009; Bao and Duong, 2012; Gouridis et al., 2015; Schuurman-Wolters et al., 2018). The dramatic difference in opening kinetics (C137) is clearly demonstrated. The correlation with reduced activity (C138) is appropriately inferred from cited literature. The generalization across multiple systems (C169) strengthens the conclusion. However, the mechanistic explanation (C170) remains somewhat inferential as the energy requirements for opening are not directly measured.

results.result: For cognate maltodextrins in wild-type MalE, a positive correlation exists between the lifetime of the closed conformation and transport/ATPase activity. Maltose, maltotriose, and maltotetraose have lifetimes of 63±6 ms, 124±4 ms, and 150±8 ms, respectively, which correlate positively with ATPase stimulation. Transport of maltotetraose is ~1.5-fold higher than maltose. This positive correlation (opposite to the negative correlation observed with mutants) implies that substrate-dependent kinetics of downstream steps after SBP opening can overcome slower opening rates, leading to preferred uptake of certain maltodextrins. This strongly suggests involvement of the translocator MalFGK2 in influencing transport rates.
results.evaluation: Claims C140-C150, C175-C176 are supported by the smFRET data in Figure 6A, E-G and Figure 6-supplement 2, combined with published ATPase and transport data (Hall et al., 1997a) shown in Figure 6H. The positive correlation (C143) is clearly demonstrated. The inference about substrate-dependent downstream steps (C146-C147) is logical given the data, though the precise molecular mechanism remains unknown (appropriately acknowledged in C148). The conclusion about translocator involvement (C150) is reasonable but somewhat speculative. The argument is strengthened by ruling out alternative explanations based on similar conformations (C149) and binding affinities.

results.result: Biological selectivity in ABC importers is achieved through a combination of mechanisms: (1) ligand release kinetics and conformational state of the SBP, and (2) selectivity provided by the translocator. The presence of substrate binding sites in translocators (well-established for the maltose system) may contribute to specificity, potentially through a proofreading mechanism analogous to aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases. The volume of binding cavities in the translocator could be a limiting factor for transport. However, the precise role of translocator binding sites in influencing transport rates remains unknown.
results.evaluation: Claims C171-C174, C178, C182-C183 represent well-reasoned conclusions and hypotheses based on the experimental data. The conclusion about combined mechanisms (C171) is strongly supported by the PsaA and MalE data. The role of the translocator (C172) is supported by the maltooctaose/maltodecaose data and citations to previous studies. However, the proofreading hypothesis (C182) and the role of translocator binding sites (C173-C174) remain speculative, appropriately acknowledged as such. The size limitation hypothesis (C178) is supported by structural data from Oldham et al., 2013. These represent reasonable interpretations of the data but would benefit from additional direct experimental validation.

results.result: Productive SBP-translocator interactions in Type I ABC importers can occur without strict structural requirements for docking, as multiple conformations activate transport. However, not all conformations facilitate transport. Substrate import can fail due to: (1) conformational mismatch where the SBP-ligand complex assumes a conformation that cannot initiate allosteric interactions with the translocator (e.g., certain non-cognate ligands in SBD1, MalE, OpuAC), or (2) conformational match but inability to open and release substrate (e.g., Zn²⁺-PsaA). The exception is OppA, which may require a unique closed conformation. Altering binding site interactions (PsaA D280N) can enable transport of otherwise non-transported ligands.
results.evaluation: Claims C158-C168 represent well-supported mechanistic conclusions synthesizing data from multiple experiments. The conclusion about flexible docking requirements (C158) is supported by the multiple-conformation data (Figure 2D-F). The conformational mismatch mechanism (C163) is supported by Figure 4D-G. The conformational match but slow opening mechanism (C167) is demonstrated by Figure 5. The exception for OppA (C159) is appropriately noted with supporting data (Figure 2-supplement 3B, citation to Doeven et al., 2008). The rescue of Zn²⁺ transport by the D280N mutation (C168) provides strong functional validation. These conclusions are logically derived from the data.

results.result: Intrinsic closing of SBPs, though rare, might influence transport in cellular contexts where SBP:translocator ratios are high. Fast (μs-ms) conformational changes may also exist as shown by NMR. In Type I ABC importers, wasteful ATP hydrolysis from thermally driven closing may be prevented by a proofreading mechanism, as substrate-free closing would not initiate translocation. This is consistent with tight coupling of ATP hydrolysis and transport in GlnPQ (which contains an internal TMD binding pocket based on homology to Art(QM)2), contrasting with futile hydrolysis in Type II importer BtuCDF (which lacks such a pocket).
results.evaluation: Claims C185-C191 represent speculative hypotheses and interpretations that extend beyond the direct experimental data. The speculation about cellular context (C185) is reasonable but not tested. The proofreading hypothesis (C187-C188) is logical but lacks direct experimental support. The correlation between TMD binding pockets and coupling efficiency (C189-C191) is based on limited examples and homology modeling (C190), not direct structural evidence for GlnPQ. While these are interesting hypotheses that fit the data, they require additional experimental validation. The citations to supporting literature (Schmidt et al., 2016; Tang et al., 2007; Lycklama A Nijeholt et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2015; Borths et al., 2005) provide some support but do not directly test these specific hypotheses.

results.result: Background and context on ABC transporters and SBPs: ABC transporters facilitate ATP-dependent trans-bilayer movement of diverse molecules with a common architecture (TMDs and NBDs). ABC importers require SBPs that share a two-lobe architecture connected by a flexible hinge. SBPs switch between open and closed conformations upon substrate binding, traditionally thought to provide transport specificity. Six SBPs were selected covering different structural clusters (PsaA-cluster A, MalE-cluster B, OppA-cluster C, SBD1/SBD2/OpuAC-cluster F) with well-characterized substrate interactions (metal ions, sugars, peptides, amino acids, compatible solutes). The hinge region is a key determinant of SBP classification and hypothesized to be important for conformational dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C46 represent well-established background knowledge supported by extensive citations to the literature (Higgins, 1992; Berntsson et al., 2010; Scheepers et al., 2016; Davidson et al., 2008; and many others). The selection of SBPs (C38-C46) is well-justified based on structural diversity and characterized substrate interactions. These claims provide appropriate context for the study and are not controversial. The traditional model of conformational switching providing specificity (C26, C29) is appropriately presented as the prevailing hypothesis that this study challenges.
